source.title: Neural Networks and Polynomial Regression. Demystifying the Overparametrization Phenomena
source.authors: Matt Emschwiller; D. Gamarnik; Eren C. Kızıldağ; Ilias Zadik

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses overparameterization and cites the reported improvement in accuracy beyond a parameter threshold, but does not measure test error across model sizes, epochs, or sample sizes, or test the other specified double-descent versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's own theoretical results concern generalization of interpolating student networks under stated assumptions, not the shape of a risk curve; these are recorded as findings that fit none of the versions. The MNIST and Fashion-MNIST experiments compare polynomial regression and CNN performance, but do not sweep model size, epochs, or training-sample size. The double-descent observation in the introduction is attributed to prior work and is not recorded as a result.
record.test_reason: The paper proves that, in a noiseless teacher/student setting, any interpolating student of any width m̂ ≥ m* generalizes once N exceeds a width-independent bound. It traces no risk curve over model size, epochs or samples, and has no interpolation-threshold peak. It cites the BHMM19 observation only as prior work. Its argument that hidden-node count is a misleading complexity measure is thematically close to V7, but it never replots a second descent against effective parameters. So it does not test V7 either.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors additionally stress that this argues against self-regularization by the training algorithm as the explanation, since every interpolating solution generalizes. They also report that degree-2 convolutional polynomial regression reaches 95.94% on MNIST and 87.11% on Fashion-MNIST.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops polynomial-regression approximations and theoretical interpolation/generalization bounds; it does not reproduce the original double-descent measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Theoretical guarantees depend on activation, depth, data-distribution assumptions, weight constraints, interpolation conditions, and sample-size bounds. The empirical polynomial-regression and CNN results vary by dataset and noise condition, but do not test the listed double-descent versions.

fits_no_version.finding: In a noiseless teacher/student setting, every interpolating student generalizes to within ε once N exceeds a bound depending only on d, L and ε. This holds regardless of student width or how interpolation is achieved.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign interpolation: with enough samples, any interpolating overparameterized network generalizes, independent of width and of implicit regularization.

record.problems: The theoretical results rely on restrictive assumptions and sample-size bounds that the authors describe as potentially very large. The empirical experiments do not vary model capacity, epochs, or sample size to test a double-descent curve.
record.rows_left_out: No other double-descent result rows were omitted. The empirical comparisons in §4 (Figure 1 and Table 1) and noise-robustness results in Figures 2–3 do not vary the axes named by the claim. The cited double-descent observation in the introduction is prior work, not a result of this study.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep of test error.
No test error over training epochs.
No sample-size sweep near the interpolation threshold. The theorems give only sufficient-N bounds.
No capacity–risk curves for any model class.
It proposes the number of regression coefficients as the complexity measure, but does not predict peak locations.
The setting is noiseless, with no label-noise or regularization sweep. Its 'noise robustness' concerns test-input perturbation.
It argues width is the wrong complexity measure, but does not replot a double-descent curve against effective parameters.

record.verdict_notes: The record's classification is accepted. The paper uses no label noise, so the V6 noise mechanism cannot arise in its setting. The §4 experiments compare methods and test robustness to input noise; none sweeps capacity, epochs or sample size.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test-error curve.
No test-error measurement over training epochs.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity-risk curves across model classes.
The paper proposes polynomial-regression coefficients as a more fitting complexity measure, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
No test of label-noise or regularization effects on double-descent peaks.
The paper argues that hidden-node count can be a misleading complexity measure, but does not replot a second-descent curve against effective parameters or show it becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.
